Claude Cahen explains the relationship between al-Maʾmūn and the Muʿtazilites in two ways. First, Hārūn al-Rashīd distrusted the Muʿtazilites, and al-Amīn did the same, so it was natural for the Muʿtazilites to side with al-Maʾmūn. Second, Cahen argues that al-Maʾmūn’s support for the Muʿtazilites was implicitly an attempt to win over the Zaydis, who were among the strongest followers of Muʿtazilism. See Claude Cahen, History of the Arabs and the Islamic Peoples, Beirut, 1972, vol. 1, p. 110. This explanation has a basis in reality, but it stays at the surface of the phenomenon and does not take account of the more powerful social factor.↩︎

Sunni Islamic law requires Muslims to obey the caliphs, based on the command in the verse: “O you who believe, obey God, obey the Messenger, and those in authority among you” (Qur’an 4:59). Jurists interpreted “those in authority” as meaning rulers.↩︎

Ḥasan Ibrāhīm Ḥasan and ʿAlī Ibrāhīm Ḥasan, Islamic Institutions, Cairo, 1970, 4th ed., p. 69. We should qualify this statement rather than accept it without restriction. Al-Mutawakkil was not “the first Abbasid caliph to love luxury.” Luxury had already accompanied the lives of Abbasid caliphs before him, just as it had accompanied the Umayyad caliphs before them. This was natural: it was an objective social phenomenon, though there were differences and exceptions, such as ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and al-Manṣūr. What distinguished al-Mutawakkil was that his love of luxury was more extravagant and excessive than that of others.↩︎
